peloneustes:enwiki:6.title: Peloneustes (Formerly assigned species and specimens, part 2)

facts.statement: The valid species of the genus Peloneustes is Peloneustes philarchus.
facts.quote: taxon: Peloneustes philarchus

facts.statement: Peloneustes philarchus was previously known by the synonyms Plesiosaurus philarchus, Thaumatosaurus philarchus, and Pliosaurus philarchus.
facts.quote: synonyms: Plesiosaurus philarchus Seeley, 1869 Thaumatosaurus philarchus (Lydekker, 1888) Pliosaurus philarchus (Seeley, 1892)

facts.statement: Peloneustes is a genus of pliosaurid plesiosaur from the Middle Jurassic of England.
facts.quote: Peloneustes (meaning mud swimmer) is a genus of pliosaurid plesiosaur from the Middle Jurassic of England.

facts.statement: Peloneustes fossils are found in the Callovian-aged Peterborough Member of the Oxford Clay Formation.
facts.quote: Its remains are known from the Peterborough Member of the Oxford Clay Formation, which is Callovian in age.

facts.statement: Peloneustes was first described as Plesiosaurus philarchus by Harry Govier Seeley in 1869 and later elevated to its own genus by Richard Lydekker in 1889.
facts.quote: It was originally described as a species of Plesiosaurus by palaeontologist Harry Govier Seeley in 1869, before being given its own genus by naturalist Richard Lydekker in 1889.

facts.statement: Peloneustes reached a total length of 3.5 to 4 meters.
facts.quote: With a total length of 3.5 – 4 m, Peloneustes is not a large pliosaurid.

facts.statement: Peloneustes had a large, triangular skull that made up about one-fifth of its body length.
facts.quote: It had a large, triangular skull, which occupied about a fifth of its body length.

facts.statement: The front of the Peloneustes skull is elongated into a narrow snout.
facts.quote: The front of the skull is elongated into a narrow rostrum (snout).

facts.statement: Peloneustes possessed conical teeth with circular cross-sections and vertical ridges on all sides.
facts.quote: The teeth of Peloneustes are conical and have circular cross-sections, bearing vertical ridges on all sides.

facts.statement: Peloneustes had a short neck consisting of only 19 to 21 cervical vertebrae.
facts.quote: With only 19 to 21 cervical (neck) vertebrae, Peloneustes had a short neck for a plesiosaur.

facts.statement: Peloneustes had flipper-like limbs where the rear pair was larger than the front pair.
facts.quote: The limbs of Peloneustes were modified into flippers, with the back pair larger than the front.

facts.statement: Peloneustes swam using a method called subaqueous flight with its flippers.
facts.quote: Peloneustes was well-adapted to aquatic life, using its flippers for a method of swimming known as subaqueous flight.

facts.statement: Peloneustes likely caught fish by swinging its narrow snout quickly and piercing them with sharp teeth.
facts.quote: The long, narrow snout of Peloneustes could have been swung quickly through the water to catch fish, which it pierced with its numerous sharp teeth.

facts.statement: Peloneustes lived in an inland sea approximately 30 to 50 meters deep.
facts.quote: Peloneustes would have inhabited an epicontinental (inland) sea that was around 30 – 50 m deep.

facts.statement: The holotype of Peloneustes philarchus was discovered by geologist Henry Porter in a clay pit near Peterborough, England.
facts.quote: Among these was the specimen which would become the holotype of Peloneustes philarchus, discovered by geologist Henry Porter in a clay pit close to Peterborough, England.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen was purchased by Adam Sedgwick in 1866 for the University of Cambridge and catalogued as CAMSM J.46913.
facts.quote: In 1866, geologist Adam Sedgwick purchased the specimen for the University of Cambridge's Woodwardian Museum (now the Sedgwick Museum of Earth Sciences, Cambridge), with the specimen being catalogued as CAMSM J.46913

facts.statement: Harry Govier Seeley described the holotype as Plesiosaurus philarchus in 1869.
facts.quote: Palaeontologist Harry Govier Seeley described the specimen as a new species of the preexisting genus Plesiosaurus, Plesiosaurus philarchus, in 1869.

facts.statement: A Peloneustes specimen catalogued as NHMUK PV R1253 was discovered in Green End, Kempston, near Bedford.
facts.quote: The specimen, catalogued under NHMUK PV R1253, had been discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation in Green End, Kempston, near Bedford.

facts.statement: Richard Lydekker published a description of the Kempston specimen as Plesiosaurus philarchus in 1889.
facts.quote: Lydekker identified this specimen as an individual of Plesiosaurus philarchus and published a description of it in 1889.

facts.statement: Richard Lydekker initially assigned the specimen to Thaumatosaurus in 1888 before creating the new genus Peloneustes in 1889.
facts.quote: He initially assigned it to Thaumatosaurus in 1888, but later decided that it was distinct enough to warrant its own genus, which he named Peloneustes in his 1889 publication.

facts.statement: Harry Govier Seeley classified Peloneustes within Pliosaurus in 1892.
facts.quote: Seeley, however, lumped Peloneustes into Pliosaurus in 1892, claiming that the two were insufficiently different to warrant separate genera.

facts.statement: Charles William Andrews described the skull anatomy of Peloneustes in 1895 using specimens from the Leeds Collection.
facts.quote: In 1895, palaeontologist Charles William Andrews described the anatomy of the skull of Peloneustes based on four partial skulls in the Leeds Collection.

facts.statement: Frédéric Jaccard published a description of Peloneustes specimens from the Musée Paléontologique de Lausanne in 1907.
facts.quote: In 1907, geologist Frédéric Jaccard published a description of two Peloneustes specimens from the Oxford Clay near Peterborough, housed in the Musée Paléontologique de Lausanne, Switzerland.

facts.statement: Hermann Linder described multiple Peloneustes specimens from German museums in 1913.
facts.quote: In 1913, naturalist Hermann Linder described multiple specimens of Peloneustes philarchus housed in the Institut für Geowissenschaften, University of Tübingen and State Museum of Natural History Stuttgart, Germany.

facts.statement: A Peloneustes specimen described by Linder had a damaged cranium but a mostly undamaged mandible.
facts.quote: Only the rear part of the cranium was in good condition, but the mandible was mostly undamaged.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Peloneustes is a close relative of Pliosaurus or a basal pliosaurid within Thalassophonea, though the latter view has more support.
facts.quote: Peloneustes has been interpreted as both a close relative of Pliosaurus or as a more basal (early-diverging) pliosaurid within Thalassophonea, with the latter interpretation finding more support.

facts.statement: The specimen NHMUK R3318 was preserved well enough to be rearticulated and mounted, though missing pelvic and limb parts were reconstructed.
facts.quote: NHMUK R3318 was so well preserved that it could be rearticulated and mounted, although the missing parts of the pelvis and limbs had to be filled in.

facts.statement: Andrews described the first skeletal mount of a pliosaurid in 1910, which provided key information about the group's anatomy.
facts.quote: Andrews had described this mount in 1910, remarking that it was the first skeletal mount of a pliosaurid, thus providing important information about the overall anatomy of the group.

facts.statement: Ketchum and Benson described the skull anatomy of Peloneustes in 2011 using more recently found specimens.
facts.quote: In 2011, palaeontologists Hilary Ketchum and Roger Benson described the anatomy of the skull of Peloneustes.

facts.statement: Seeley named the species Plesiosaurus sterrodeirus in the same publication where he named Peloneustes philarchus, based on cranial and vertebral material.
facts.quote: In the same publication in which he named P. philarchus, Seeley also named another species of Plesiosaurus, P. sterrodeirus based on seven specimens in the Woodwardian Museum consisting of cranial and vertebral material.

facts.statement: Lydekker reclassified Plesiosaurus sterrodeirus and Pleiosaurus aequalis into the genus Peloneustes when he established the genus for P. philarchus.
facts.quote: When Lydekker erected the genus Peloneustes for P. philarchus, he also reclassified "Plesiosaurus" sterrodeirus and "Pleiosaurus" aequalis (a species named by John Phillips in 1871) as members of this genus.

facts.statement: Tarlo suggested that Peloneustes sterrodeirus actually belongs to the genus Pliosaurus, possibly as a synonym of P. brachydeirus.
facts.quote: He considered Peloneustes sterrodeirus to instead belong to Pliosaurus, possibly within P. brachydeirus.

facts.statement: Lydekker reassigned Pliosaurus evansi to Peloneustes in 1890, noting it was larger than P. philarchus despite being a smaller Pliosaurus species.
facts.quote: Due to it being a smaller species of Pliosaurus and its similarity to Peloneustes philarchus, Lydekker reassigned it to Peloneustes in 1890, noting that it was larger than Peloneustes philarchus.

facts.statement: Andrews assigned a partial skeleton of a large pliosaur to Peloneustes evansi in 1913, distinguishing it from P. philarchus based on mandible and vertebrae differences.
facts.quote: In 1913, Andrews assigned a partial skeleton of another large pliosaur found by Leeds to Peloneustes evansi, noting that while the mandible and vertebrae were similar to other Peloneustes evansi specimens, they were quite different from those of Peloneustes philarchus.

facts.statement: Andrews hypothesized that Peloneustes evansi might belong to a separate genus intermediate between Peloneustes and Pliosaurus.
facts.quote: Consequently, Andrews considered it possible that P. evansi really belonged to a separate genus that was morphologically intermediate between Peloneustes and Pliosaurus.

facts.statement: Tarlo synonymized Peloneustes evansi with P. philarchus in 1960 because their cervical vertebrae were identical except for size differences.
facts.quote: In his 1960 review of pliosaurids, Tarlo synonymised Peloneustes evansi with Peloneustes philarchus due to their cervical vertebrae being identical (save for a difference in size).

facts.statement: Tarlo assigned larger specimens of Peloneustes evansi to a new species Pliosaurus andrewsi, though this species is no longer considered part of Pliosaurus.
facts.quote: He considered the larger specimens of Peloneustes evansi distinct, and assigned them to a new species of Pliosaurus, P. andrewsi (although this species is no longer considered to belong in Pliosaurus).

facts.statement: Ketchum and Benson argued in 2011 that Peloneustes evansi is a nomen dubium because its holotype lacks distinguishing features.
facts.quote: Hilary F. Ketchum and Roger B. J. Benson disagreed with this synonymy, and in 2011 considered that since the holotype of Peloneustes evansi is nondiagnostic (lacking distinguishing features), P. evansi is a nomen dubium and therefore an indeterminate pliosaurid.

facts.statement: Koken described Plesiosaurus kanzleri in 1905 based on two Early Cretaceous dorsal vertebrae found near Gronau, Germany.
facts.quote: In 1905, palaeontologist Ernst Koken described another species of Plesiosaurus, P. kanzleri, from two Early Cretaceous dorsal vertebrae discovered in a clay pit near Gronau, northern Germany.

facts.statement: Koken suggested that Plesiosaurus kanzleri might belong to Peloneustes based on vertebral morphology.
facts.quote: He nevertheless suggested that this species might belong to Peloneustes, owing to the morphology of these vertebrae.

facts.statement: Linder created the subspecies Peloneustes philarchus var. spathyrhynchus in 1913 based on a spatulate mandibular symphysis.
facts.quote: In 1913, Linder created a subspecies of Peloneustes, P. philarchus var. spathyrhynchus, differentiating it based on its spatulate mandibular symphysis (where the two sides of the mandible meet and fuse).

facts.statement: Tarlo synonymized the subspecies P. philarchus var. spathyrhynchus in 1960, attributing the wider mandibular symphysis to intraspecific variation.
facts.quote: Tarlo considered it to be a synonym of Peloneustes philarchus in 1960, and the mandibular symphysis of Peloneustes is proportionately wider in larger specimens, making this trait more likely to be due to intraspecific variation (variation within species).

facts.statement: Riabinin tentatively assigned material from Kostroma Oblast and Hooker Island to Peloneustes philarchus in 1909 and 1936, but these assignments are now doubted.
facts.quote: In 1909 and 1936, respectively, palaeontologist Anatoly Riabinin described material from the Callovian or Oxfordian of Kostroma Oblast and the Oxfordian of Hooker Island, Franz Josef Land, which he tentatively assigned to Peloneustes philarchus; however, these assignments have since been doubted.

facts.statement: Huene assigned a fragmentary tooth from Courland to Peloneustes sp. in 1937, but Ketchum and Benson rejected this assignment in 2011.
facts.quote: In 1937, Friedrich von Huene assigned a fragmentary tooth possibly dating from the Callovian and coming from the Baltic region of Courland to Peloneustes sp., but this assignment was rejected by Ketchum and Benson in 2011.

facts.statement: Novozhilov named Peloneustes irgisensis in 1948 based on specimen PIN 426, a partial skeleton with preserved stomach contents.
facts.quote: In 1948, palaeontologist Nestor Novozhilov named a new species of Peloneustes, P. irgisensis, based on PIN 426, a partial skeleton consisting of a large, incomplete skull, vertebrae, and a partial hind limb, with stomach contents preserved.

facts.statement: Tarlo tentatively placed Peloneustes irgisensis in Pliosaurus in 1960, considering it too different from P. philarchus.
facts.quote: In his 1960 review, Tarlo considered this species to be too different from Peloneustes philarchus to belong to Peloneustes, tentatively placing it in Pliosaurus.

facts.statement: Novozhilov erected the genus Strongylokrotaphus for P. irgisensis in 1964, but later studies reassigned it to Pliosaurus, possibly as a synonym of P. rossicus.
facts.quote: In 1964 Novozhilov erected a new genus, Strongylokrotaphus, for this species, but further studies concurred with Tarlo and reassigned the species to Pliosaurus, possibly a synonym of Pliosaurus rossicus.

facts.statement: Recent studies consider Peloneustes irgisensis a nomen dubium but recommend a new description of the holotype.
facts.quote: More recent studies considered the taxon as a nomen dubium given its currently undiagnostic character, but nevertheless recommend a new description of the holotype.

facts.statement: A new description of the holotype of P. irgisensis is risky due to severe damage from pyrite decay and loss of associated elements.
facts.quote: However, this suggestion risks being tainted by the current state of conservation of specimen PIN 426, the skull and notably the mandible having since been seriously damaged by pyrite decay, and the associated elements being noted as lost.

facts.statement: Maryańska attributed cranial fragments found in an Oxfordian quarry in Załęcze Wielkie, Poland, to Peloneustes sp. in 1972.
facts.quote: In 1972, paleontologist Teresa Maryańska attributed cranial fragments to Peloneustes sp. which were discovered in an Oxfordian quarry in Załęcze Wielkie, Poland.

facts.statement: Ketchum and Benson reidentified the Załęcze Wielkie specimen as an undetermined marine teleosaurid crocodylomorph in 2011.
facts.quote: In 2011, Ketchum and Benson reidentified this specimen as actually coming from an undetermined marine teleosaurid crocodylomorph.

facts.statement: O'Keefe proposed in 1998 that a pliosaurid from the Lower Jurassic Posidonia Shale of Germany might be a new Peloneustes species.
facts.quote: In 1998, palaeontologist Frank Robin O'Keefe proposed that a pliosaurid specimen from the Lower Jurassic Posidonia Shale of Germany might represent a new species of Peloneustes.

facts.statement: O'Keefe reclassified the specimen as Hauffiosaurus zanoni in 2001, placing it in a separate genus.
facts.quote: However, in 2001, he considered it to belong to a separate genus and species, naming it Hauffiosaurus zanoni.

facts.statement: Gasparini and Iturralde-Vinent assigned a pliosaurid from the Upper Jurassic Jagua Formation of Cuba to Peloneustes sp. in 2006.
facts.quote: Palaeontologists Zulma Gasparini and Manuel A. Iturralde-Vinent assigned a pliosaurid from the Upper Jurassic Jagua Formation of Cuba to Peloneustes sp. in 2006.

facts.statement: Gasparini redescribed the Cuban pliosaurid as Gallardosaurus iturraldei in 2009.
facts.quote: In 2009, Gasparini redescribed it as Gallardosaurus iturraldei.

facts.statement: Ketchum and Benson concluded in 2011 that Peloneustes contains only the single species P. philarchus.
facts.quote: In 2011, Ketchum and Benson considered Peloneustes to contain only one species, P. philarchus.

facts.statement: Ketchum and Benson suggested that some specimens from the Peterborough Member and Marquise, France, previously assigned to Peloneustes belong to unnamed pliosaurids.
facts.quote: They considered some specimens from the Peterborough Member and Marquise, France previously assigned to Peloneustes to belong to different, currently unnamed pliosaurids.

facts.statement: Peloneustes is classified as a small to medium-sized pliosaurid.
facts.quote: Peloneustes is a small- to medium-sized member of Pliosauridae.

facts.statement: A mounted skeleton of Peloneustes at the Natural History Museum in London measures 11.5 feet in length.
facts.quote: NHMUK R3318, the mounted skeleton in the Natural History Museum in London, is 11.5 ft long

facts.statement: Specimen GPIT-RE-3182 is estimated to have reached a body length of approximately 4.34 meters and a mass of around 1 metric ton during its lifetime.
facts.quote: This latter, numbered as GPIT-RE-3182, would have reached an estimated body length of approximately 4.34 m during its lifetime, for a body mass of around 1 MT.

facts.statement: Peloneustes belongs to the large-headed, short-necked pliosauromorph morphotype, with its skull comprising slightly less than one-fifth of its total body length.
facts.quote: Peloneustes is of the latter morphotype, with its skull making up a little less than a fifth of the animal's total length.

facts.statement: Peloneustes possessed a short tail, a massive torso, and limbs modified into large flippers.
facts.quote: Peloneustes, like all plesiosaurs, had a short tail, massive torso, and all of its limbs modified into large flippers.

facts.statement: The crania of Peloneustes vary in length between 60 and 78.5 centimeters.
facts.quote: These crania vary in size, measuring 60 - 78.5 cm in length.

facts.statement: The Peloneustes cranium is elongated and slopes upwards toward the rear.
facts.quote: The cranium of Peloneustes is elongated, and slopes upwards towards its back end.

facts.statement: The external nares of Peloneustes are small and located approximately halfway along the length of the cranium.
facts.quote: The external nares (openings for the nostrils) are small and located about halfway along the length of the cranium.

facts.statement: The scleral rings of Peloneustes consist of at least 16 individual elements, which is unusually high for a reptile.
facts.quote: The scleral rings are composed of at least 16 individual elements, an unusually high number for a reptile.

facts.statement: The temporal fenestrae of Peloneustes are enlarged, elliptical, and situated on the rearmost quarter of the cranium.
facts.quote: The temporal fenestrae (openings in the back of the cranium) are enlarged, elliptical, and located on the cranium's rearmost quarter.

facts.statement: The premaxillae of Peloneustes characteristically bear six teeth each.
facts.quote: Characteristically, the premaxillae (front upper tooth-bearing bones) of Peloneustes bear six teeth each

facts.statement: The longest mandible of Peloneustes measures 87.7 centimeters.
facts.quote: The longest of these measures 87.7 cm.

facts.statement: Each dentary of Peloneustes contains between 36 and 44 teeth, with 13 to 15 located on the symphysis.
facts.quote: Each dentary (the tooth-bearing bone in the mandible) has between 36 and 44 teeth, 13 to 15 of which are located on the symphysis.

facts.statement: The elevated ridge on the mandibular symphysis where the dentaries meet is a unique feature of Peloneustes not found in other plesiosaurs.
facts.quote: This is a unique feature of Peloneustes, not seen in any other plesiosaurs.

facts.statement: The teeth of Peloneustes have circular cross-sections, a trait shared with other pliosaurids of its age.
facts.quote: The teeth of Peloneustes have circular cross sections, as seen in other pliosaurids of its age.

facts.statement: The teeth of Peloneustes are shaped like recurved cones.
facts.quote: The teeth have the shape of recurved cones.

facts.statement: Peloneustes has heterodont dentition, meaning it possesses teeth of different shapes.
facts.quote: The dentition of Peloneustes is heterodont, that is, it has teeth of different shapes.

facts.statement: Peloneustes has larger caniniform teeth at the front of the jaws and smaller, sharper, stouter teeth further back.
facts.quote: The larger teeth are caniniform and located at the front of the jaws, while the smaller teeth are more sharply recurved, stouter, and located further back.

facts.statement: Andrews reported in 1913 that Peloneustes possessed 21 to 22 cervical, 2 to 3 pectoral, and approximately 20 dorsal vertebrae based on specimens from the Leeds Collection.
facts.quote: In 1913, Andrews reported that Peloneustes had 21 to 22 cervical, 2 to 3 pectoral, and around 20 dorsal vertebrae, with the exact number of sacral (hip) and caudal vertebrae unknown, based on specimens in the Leeds Collection.

facts.statement: In adult Peloneustes, the first two cervical vertebrae (atlas and axis) are fused, whereas in juveniles they exist as separate unfused elements.
facts.quote: The first two cervical vertebrae, the atlas and axis, are fused in adults, but in juveniles they are present as several unfused elements.

facts.statement: The cervical vertebrae of Peloneustes feature tall neural spines that are compressed laterally.
facts.quote: The cervical vertebrae bear tall neural spines that are compressed from side to side.

facts.statement: Andrews hypothesized in 1913 that the tail morphology of Peloneustes stiffened the tail to support its large hind limbs.
facts.quote: Andrews hypothesised in 1913 that this configuration would have stiffened the tail, possibly to support the large hind limbs.

facts.statement: Andrews speculated in 1913 that the tail morphology of Peloneustes supported a small tail fin-like structure.
facts.quote: In 1913, Andrews speculated that this morphology may have been present to support a small tail fin-like structure.

facts.statement: Peloneustes had hind limbs longer than its forelimbs, with the femur longer than the humerus, though the humerus was more robust.
facts.quote: The hind limbs of Peloneustes are longer than its forelimbs, with the femur being longer than the humerus, although the humerus is the more robust of the two elements.

facts.statement: Benson and Druckenmiller identified Peloneustes as the most basal member of the clade Thalassophonea in 2013.
facts.quote: In 2013, Benson and palaeontologist Patrick S. Druckenmiller named a new clade within Pliosauridae, Thalassophonea. This clade included the "classic", short-necked pliosaurids while excluding the earlier, long-necked, more gracile forms. Peloneustes was found to be the most basal thalassophonean.

facts.statement: Peloneustes lived during the Middle Jurassic period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Jurásico Medio

facts.statement: Peloneustes lived during the Middle Jurassic (Callovian) in what is now Great Britain.
facts.quote: Peloneustes (nadador del fango) es un género representado por una única especie de pliosauroide pliosáurido, que vivió en el Jurásico Medio (Calloviense) en lo que ahora es Gran Bretaña.

facts.statement: Fossils of Peloneustes were found in the Oxford Clay formation, which dates to the early Oxfordian stage.
facts.quote: Sus restos se encontraron en la formación Oxford Clay, que data de principios del Oxfordiense

facts.statement: The diet of Peloneustes may have consisted of hard-shelled ammonites, belemnites, squids, cuttlefish, and other marine reptiles.
facts.quote: Su dieta pudo estar basada en ammonites de concha dura, belemnites, sepias, calamares y otros reptiles marinos.

facts.statement: Peloneustes is one of the smallest genera in its family, reaching lengths of up to 3 meters.
facts.quote: Es uno de los géneros más pequeños de la familia, de hasta 3 metros de longitud.

facts.statement: Peloneustes lived between 165.3 and 161.5 million years ago during the Callovian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Callovian to Callovian (165.3 to 161.5 million years ago)

facts.statement: The parent group of Peloneustes is Thalassophonea.
facts.quote: Parent group: Thalassophonea

facts.statement: Peloneustes belongs to the family Pliosauridae.
facts.quote: Family: Pliosauridae

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Peloneustes is Peloneustes philarchus.
facts.quote: Type species: Peloneustes philarchus

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding the relationships of pliosaurids; White (1940) suggested they were close relatives of Elasmosauridae, while Welles (1943) argued they were more similar to Polycotylidae.
facts.quote: In 1940, palaeontologist Theodore E. White considered pliosaurids to be close relatives of Elasmosauridae based on shoulder anatomy. However, in 1943, palaeontologist Samuel P. Welles thought that pliosaurids were more similar to Polycotylidae, as they both had large skulls and short necks, among other characteristics.

facts.statement: The phylogenetic position of Peloneustes within Pliosauridae is debated, with O'Keefe (2001) placing it as a basal member outside a specific group, while Smith and Dyke (2008) identified it as the sister taxon to Pliosaurus.
facts.quote: In 2001, O'Keefe recovered it as a basal (early-diverging) member of this family, outside of a group including Liopleurodon, Pliosaurus, and Brachauchenius. However, in 2008, palaeontologists Adam S. Smith and Gareth J. Dyke found Peloneustes to be the sister taxon of Pliosaurus.

rejected.statement: Andrews described the anatomy of Peloneustes based on well-preserved skulls and an almost complete skeleton in his 1913 publication.
rejected.quote: The anatomy of the Peloneustes specimens was described in the second volume, based primarily on the well-preserved skulls NHMUK R2679 and NHMUK R3808 and NHMUK R3318, an almost complete skeleton.

rejected.statement: The discovery of specimen NHMUK R4058, a skull preserved in three dimensions, improved understanding of Peloneustes skull shape after earlier studies.
rejected.quote: Since the previous anatomical studies of Andrews and Linder, more specimens had been found, including NHMUK R4058, a skull preserved in three dimensions, providing a better idea of the skull's shape.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'R 4058 a skull preserved in three dimensions'

rejected.statement: Sachs and colleagues concluded in 2016 that Plesiosaurus kanzleri remains a nomen dubium due to lack of diagnostic characters.
rejected.quote: They nevertheless emphasized that the material lacks a diagnostic combination of characters that would allow a confident taxonomic assignment, and P. kanzleri therefore remains a nomen dubium.

rejected.statement: Ketchum and Benson recognized 21 definite specimens of Peloneustes philarchus, all from the Peterborough Member of the Oxford Clay Formation.
rejected.quote: They recognised twenty one definite specimens of Peloneustes philarchus, all from the Peterborough Member of the Oxford Clay Formation.

rejected.statement: Viewed from above, the Peloneustes cranium is shaped like an isosceles triangle with a broad rear and a narrow, elongated front rostrum.
rejected.quote: Viewed from above, the cranium is shaped like an isosceles triangle, with the back of the cranium broad and the front elongated into a narrow rostrum.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'cranium is shaped like an isosceles triangle with'

rejected.statement: In Peloneustes, the frontals contact both the eye sockets and the external nares, a distinctive trait of the genus.
rejected.quote: The frontals (bones bordering the eye sockets) of Peloneustes contact both the eye sockets and the external nares, a distinctive trait of Peloneustes.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'contact both the eye sockets and the external'

rejected.statement: Lydekker assigned Peloneustes to the family Pliosauridae in 1890, a classification that has remained consistent.
rejected.quote: Lydekker placed Peloneustes in this family, to which it has been consistently assigned since.
